extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of political theory, history, and institutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Critical analysis of constitutional and institutional arrangements (checks and balances, representation, guild socialism) addressing how political systems mediate local interests, information flow, coercion, and democratic representation. Emphasizes practical effects of design choices and transition dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances to equilibrate special interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Special interests should be kept in equilibrium by a balance of power: 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Constitution's designers intended to deadlock local and class interests so they would not obstruct government; checks and balances are presented as a remedy for the problem of public opinion and as a substitute for direct popular consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable government to control the governed while obliging it to control itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The design must 'first enable the government to control the governed, and in the next place, oblige it to control itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional arrangements should provide both authoritative capacity and internal restraints; this dual requirement shaped features like separation of powers and veto/judicial checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the sphere of popular rule with institutional checks
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution was intended as a candid attempt to limit popular rule, making the House the only democratic organ with a suffrage highly limited by property qualifications, and checking it by Senate, electoral college, Presidential veto, and judicial interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers may purposely constrain direct popular power; evaluating a constitution requires noting which organs are democratic and what countervailing mechanisms restrain them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal acceptance requires alignment of constitutional meaning with public sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution that frankly denies popular rule will not long be tolerated; practice, amendment, or reinterpretation may be necessary to align the text with prevailing moral feeling (e.g., Jefferson's re-framing of the Constitution as democratic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate not just text but how a constitution is read and practiced; legitimacy and survival often depend on adapting form to popular expectations through rhetoric, practice, and amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage as a mechanism to bind local leaders to national government
rubrics_metrics.description: Patronage and rotation in office (turning public office into patronage) served to wean local leaders from parochialism and attach them to the national government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although ostensible reforms (rotation, short terms) aimed at democratization, in practice patronage created a new governing class and stabilized the union; assess practical political incentives, not only stated ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative bodies require systematic information and analytical instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislature composed of local representatives is insufficient for national policy unless it has systematic, adequate, and authorized ways to know national conditions (controlled reporting and objective analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislatures need bureaus, expert bodies, data, and reporting mechanisms (analogous to executive departmental bureaus or independent commissions) to make informed decisions; absence leads to reliance on partisan insiders, private tips, or sensational investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing national legislation on fragmented local bargaining or logrolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Without effective means of information and analysis, legislation becomes either prepared by a few informed insiders or broken into collections of local items enacted for local reasons, producing logrolling and pork-barrel politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether legislative outcomes reflect comprehensive policy-making or are the product of reciprocal local bargains; prefer institutional designs that reduce fragmentation and make cumulative costs transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-building depends on development of common consciousness (information) rather than coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperation among large groups depends on the degree to which material for a common consciousness exists; where common knowledge is lacking, cooperation relies on patronage/force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prospects for federations, leagues, or industrial governance by measuring information flows and shared understanding rather than assuming voluntary cooperation alone will suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any claimed 'non-coercive' polity must specify retained coercive powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Guild-socialist proposals promise non-coercion yet assign to the Commune powers (fixing prices, allocating credit, levying taxes, conferring coercive powers, declaring war, running police) that are coercive in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize purportedly non-coercive institutional plans for enumerated powers; evaluate the real coercive instruments required for governance and their implications for liberty and centralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for transition dynamics and the likely need for force
rubrics_metrics.description: Even proponents of Guild Socialism acknowledge that the transition cannot be achieved by universal consent and anticipate direct action or force (trade-union action, possible civil conflict).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate schemes for systemic change by explicitly considering transitional coercion, instability, and how initial methods of change shape the future institutional character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic units should be at the scale of familiar, directly known environments
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural democratic unit is a familiar environment (factory/shop, mines, docks, stations) where 'men are really in personal contact' and can exercise self-government directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proposals by whether the units of representation are small enough for direct participation and knowledge; recognize that many important matters (wages, markets, planning) transcend the shop scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-level coordination is necessary because shop-level opinions do not cover translocal affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Shop democracy can handle matters 'taken in at a single view' but cannot by itself manage external relations (marketing, inter-shop coordination, industry-wide planning), which require federal structures and coordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating decentralized democratic proposals, test their mechanisms for representing and resolving conflicts that cross unit boundaries and require aggregated knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional representation vs territorial representation — limits and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Guildsmen propose representatives who act for particular functions rather than territorially; each person helps choose multiple representatives for distinct essential functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether function-based representation actually enables candid voting according to known interests and whether it provides standards for judging proposals that transcend narrow function-specific experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representatives need education, information, or propaganda to form views beyond direct experience
rubrics_metrics.description: A shop's public opinions about its duties in the industry or society are matters of education or propaganda; representatives cannot reliably generalize from narrow shop experience to wider policy without additional information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the informational and civic-education mechanisms provided to delegates in any representative scheme; absence will produce misinformed generalizations and poor decisions on translocal issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional design must include mechanisms to maintain equality and prevent re-emergence of class power
rubrics_metrics.description: Abolition of capitalist property alone is insufficient; guildsmen insist institutions must be built to maintain equilibrium and the 'mechanism right' to express men's social wills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically assess whether proposed institutional mechanisms are capable of sustaining equality over time, including how budgets, allocation of income, and enforcement will be handled to avoid concentration of power.
